reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: A congenital lymphatic malformation that most often presents as a soft, compressible, painless swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck or the axilla
The lesion characteristically transilluminates brightly because it is filled with clear lymphatic fluid
Many are detected antenatally or in early infancy; fetal nuchal cystic hygroma is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner and Down syndromes
The swelling may enlarge suddenly following intracystic bleeding or with an upper respiratory infection
Large cervical lesions can extend toward the floor of the mouth or mediastinum and threaten the airway or swallowing
Ultrasound and MRI define the extent and whether the lesion is macrocystic or microcystic, guiding treatment choice
Management options include sclerotherapy (often effective for macrocystic lesions) and surgical excision, though complete removal can be difficult when the malformation infiltrates vital structures
Because the malformation crosses tissue planes and encases nerves and vessels, incomplete excision and recurrence are common
reference.pathophysiology: Cystic hygroma is a malformation of the lymphatic system in which sequestered lymphatic channels fail to connect normally with the venous drainage, producing dilated, fluid-filled cystic spaces. These may be macrocystic (large cysts) or microcystic and tend to infiltrate along tissue planes rather than respect anatomical boundaries. Accumulated lymph distends the cysts, and intralesional haemorrhage or infection can cause rapid, sometimes dangerous, enlargement. The malformation grows with the child and does not spontaneously regress in most cases.
additionalInvestigations: Neck and soft-tissue ultrasound to confirm the cystic nature and transillumination correlate
MRI to map the full extent and involvement of adjacent structures
Antenatal ultrasound and karyotyping when detected in the fetus
Airway assessment (including nasendoscopy or cross-sectional imaging) for large cervical lesions
Assessment for associated syndromes when clinically indicated
redFlags: Airway compromise from a large or rapidly enlarging cervical or oral lesion, which may be life-threatening
Sudden painful swelling due to intracystic haemorrhage
Signs of infection within the malformation causing rapid expansion
Feeding or swallowing difficulty from mass effect on the pharynx
reference.prognosis: Small, well-localised macrocystic lesions often respond well to sclerotherapy or excision. Extensive, infiltrative, or microcystic malformations are harder to eradicate, recur frequently, and may require repeated interventions. Fetal cystic hygromas associated with chromosomal or cardiac anomalies carry a guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Attempting aggressive complete excision at the cost of damaging encased nerves and vessels
Underestimating airway risk in large cervical lesions before intervention
Assuming the lesion will spontaneously resolve, unlike infantile haemangiomas
Overlooking associated chromosomal or cardiac anomalies in antenatally detected cases
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
